Use older Debian with libtool 1.5.x which supports mode inference

non_solutions: Regenerating with automake will not help if the project uses custom libtool invocations without --mode

summary: Deprecated libltdl APIs removed in libtool 2.1b cause compile or link failures for projects using them
mechanism: Libtool 2.1b (first stable release: 2.2) removed the following deprecated libltdl APIs: lt_dlcaller_register, lt_dlhandle_next, lt_dlhandle_find, lt_dlforeach, lt_dlmutex_register, lt_dlmutex_lock, lt_dlmutex_unlock, lt_dlmutex_seterror, lt_dlmutex_geterror, lt_dlmalloc, lt_dlrealloc, lt_dlfree. Projects using these functions will fail to compile (implicit declaration) or link (undefined reference).

actions.hint: Replace lt_dlmalloc/lt_dlfree/lt_dlrealloc with standard malloc/free/realloc. Replace lt_dlmutex_* with platform threading primitives. Replace lt_dlhandle_next with lt_dlhandle_iterate. Replace lt_dlforeach with lt_dlhandle_map.
Use older Debian with libtool 1.5.x which still provides these APIs

non_solutions: Relinking or rerunning libtoolize will not restore the removed API symbols

summary: The -static link flag now only affects uninstalled libraries, changing linking behavior and potentially causing unresolved symbol errors
mechanism: In libtool 2.1b (first stable release: 2.2), the -static link flag was fixed to only link uninstalled libraries statically. Previously -static would force static linking of all libtool libraries. Projects relying on -static to force static linking of installed libraries will now get shared linking instead, which can cause unresolved symbols if the shared library is not available or has different symbol visibility. The new flag -static-libtool-libs provides the old -static semantics.
trigger_patterns: libtool: link: cannot find the library

actions.hint: Replace -static with -static-libtool-libs in LDFLAGS or _LDFLAGS if the intent is to statically link all libtool libraries
Use older Debian with libtool 1.5.x where -static forces static linking of all libtool libraries

non_solutions: Using LDFLAGS=-static affects the system linker, not libtool's library selection

summary: AC_PROG_LIBTOOL macro is obsolete since libtool 2.2; projects using it may get warnings that escalate to errors with newer autoconf/automake combinations.
mechanism: Libtool 2.2 (first stable release of the 2.x series) replaced AC_PROG_LIBTOOL, AM_PROG_LIBTOOL, AC_LIBTOOL_DLOPEN, and AC_LIBTOOL_WIN32_DLL with the unified LT_INIT macro. The old macros are provided as thin compatibility wrappers that emit deprecation warnings. When combined with automake's -Werror or autoconf's stricter macro handling in 2.70+, these warnings can become fatal errors during autoreconf.

actions.hint: Replace AC_PROG_LIBTOOL or AM_PROG_LIBTOOL with LT_INIT in configure.ac. Replace AC_LIBTOOL_DLOPEN with LT_INIT([dlopen]). Replace AC_ENABLE_SHARED/AC_DISABLE_SHARED with LT_INIT([shared])/LT_INIT([disable-shared]).
Use older Debian with libtool 1.5.x where AC_PROG_LIBTOOL is the primary interface

non_solutions: Simply suppressing the warning with -Wno-obsolete does not fix the underlying incompatibility with newer autoconf

summary: LT_WITH_LTDL macro was renamed to LTDL_INIT in libtool 2.2, causing undefined macro errors for projects using the old name.
mechanism: Libtool 2.1b/2.2 renamed the LT_WITH_LTDL macro to LTDL_INIT as part of the libltdl API overhaul. Projects with LT_WITH_LTDL in their configure.ac will get an undefined macro error when running autoreconf with libtool >= 2.2 m4 files installed.

actions.hint: Replace LT_WITH_LTDL with LTDL_INIT in configure.ac
Use older Debian with libtool 1.5.x where LT_WITH_LTDL is the correct macro

summary: Libtool-using projects fail bootstrap when libtoolize was not run or LT_INIT/AM_PROG_AR macro setup is missing.
mechanism: Automake emits hard errors such as missing ltmain.sh or LIBTOOL undefined when Makefile.am declares libtool libraries but configure.ac/libtoolize setup is incomplete.

actions.hint: Add AC_CONFIG_MACRO_DIRS([m4]), AM_PROG_AR, and LT_INIT as needed, then run libtoolize --copy --force and autoreconf -fi.

summary: libtoolize uses GNU m4 tracing; missing or non-GNU m4 can abort bootstrap.
mechanism: Newer libtoolize traces configure.ac using GNU m4 to infer macro and directory setup. Environments with no m4 or incompatible m4 fail before ltmain.sh and macros are installed.

actions.hint: Install GNU m4 and ensure M4/PATH points to it before running libtoolize/autoreconf.

summary: AC_CONFIG_MACRO_DIRS adoption can break rebootstrap with old Autoconf/Automake combinations.
mechanism: In libtool 2.4.3, libtoolize began advising use of the new Autoconf AC_CONFIG_MACRO_DIRS declaration. Per the libtool 2.4.3 NEWS, following that advice requires all developers to have at least autoconf-2.70 and automake-1.13 to rebootstrap the project; older Autotools report an undefined AC_CONFIG_MACRO_DIRS macro or aclocal directory failures. The NEWS documents a m4_ifndef compatibility shim (defining AC_CONFIG_MACRO_DIRS from AC_CONFIG_MACRO_DIR) to keep older-bootstrap support.

actions.hint: Use the documented m4_ifndef compatibility shim for AC_CONFIG_MACRO_DIRS or bootstrap with Autoconf >= 2.70 and Automake >= 1.13.

summary: libtoolize errors when ACLOCAL_AMFLAGS and AC_CONFIG_MACRO_DIR point at inconsistent macro directories.
mechanism: Old projects often carry both ACLOCAL_AMFLAGS=-I m4 and AC_CONFIG_MACRO_DIR with another path. libtoolize can refuse this conflicting macro-dir setup.

actions.hint: Make AC_CONFIG_MACRO_DIR(S) and ACLOCAL_AMFLAGS -I use the same directory, preferably m4, then rerun autoreconf -fi.

summary: gettext 0.10.35 changed msgunfmt interface and deprecated tupdate in favor of msgmerge
mechanism: Build scripts calling msgunfmt with old interface or using tupdate will fail. Projects using po/Makefile.in.in with tupdate references will break.
trigger_patterns: (tupdate): (command not found|No such file or directory)

actions.hint: Replace tupdate invocations with msgmerge in build scripts and po/Makefile.in.in
Use gettext < 0.10.35

non_solutions: Cannot install tupdate separately as it has been removed from gettext

summary: gettext 0.11 deprecated @INTLLIBS@ Makefile variable, replaced by @LIBINTL@ or @LTLIBINTL@.
mechanism: The Makefile variable @INTLLIBS@ is deprecated. It is replaced with @LIBINTL@ (in projects without libtool) or @LTLIBINTL@ (in projects with libtool). Projects still using @INTLLIBS@ may get empty substitution.

actions.hint: Use gettext < 0.11 where @INTLLIBS@ is still supported

non_solutions: Source code changes alone will not fix build system macro deprecation

summary: gettext 0.20 removed the --intl gettextize option and AM_GNU_GETTEXT_INTL_SUBDIR macro
mechanism: Projects that use AM_GNU_GETTEXT_INTL_SUBDIR in configure.ac or rely on gettextize --intl will fail during autoreconf with undefined macro errors. The intl/ bundling approach is no longer supported.

actions.hint: Remove AM_GNU_GETTEXT_INTL_SUBDIR from configure.ac and run autoreconf
Use gettext < 0.20

non_solutions: Cannot restore --intl support as it has been permanently removed from gettext

summary: msgfmt --check now enforces format string consistency in plural forms, causing build failures for PO files that omit format specifiers in msgstr[N]
mechanism: Starting with gettext 0.15, msgfmt's format string checking (-c/--check flag) became stricter for plural forms. Previously, a plural translation could omit format specifiers (e.g., msgstr[0] without %d when msgid has %d) without error. Now msgfmt -c rejects such translations. Since the standard automake po/Makefile.in.in invokes msgfmt with -c by default, old PO files with format string mismatches in plural forms will cause build failures when compiled with gettext >= 0.15.
trigger_patterns: number of format specifications in 'msgid' and 'msgstr\[

actions.hint: Fix the PO file to include matching format specifiers in all msgstr[N] plural forms, or remove the -c flag from MSGFMT invocation in po/Makefile
Use older Debian with gettext < 0.15

non_solutions: Removing the c-format flag from the msgid will suppress the check but may hide real translation bugs

summary: AM_GNU_GETTEXT_INTL_SUBDIR macro was removed in gettext 0.20, causing configure failures for projects that use it
mechanism: In gettext 0.20, the --intl option of gettextize (deprecated since 0.18/2010) was fully removed, and the Autoconf macro AM_GNU_GETTEXT_INTL_SUBDIR was removed along with it. Projects that have AM_GNU_GETTEXT_INTL_SUBDIR in their configure.ac will fail during autoreconf because aclocal cannot find the macro definition, resulting in an undefined macro error during autoconf processing.

actions.hint: Remove AM_GNU_GETTEXT_INTL_SUBDIR from configure.ac. Use AM_GNU_GETTEXT([external]) instead of bundling intl sources, and remove the intl/ subdirectory from the project.
Use older Debian with gettext < 0.20

non_solutions: Adding AC_DEFUN for AM_GNU_GETTEXT_INTL_SUBDIR as a stub - this may silence the macro error but the intl subdirectory infrastructure is gone

summary: m4 1.4.21 `eval' rejects incomplete integer literals like `0x' instead of silently treating them as 0
mechanism: Starting with m4 1.4.21 the `eval' builtin conforms to C integer-literal rules: an input such as `eval(0x)' (a hex prefix with no following digits) is no longer coerced to 0 but flagged as a malformed expression, drawing on the same `bad expression in eval' diagnostic family m4 already used for other malformed eval input (e.g. `bad expression in eval (excess input)'). If an autoconf/acinclude.m4 macro feeds a possibly-empty radix literal into eval, the configure regeneration (autoreconf) now aborts with a non-zero exit status where it previously produced output. (m4 also supports `0b'/`0r' radix prefixes that would be rejected analogously, but the 1.4.21 NEWS entry names only `0x'.)

actions.hint: In the offending m4 macro (configure.ac / acinclude.m4 / *.m4), make radix literals well-formed, e.g. emit `0x0' / `0b0' instead of the bare `0x' / `0b' produced from an empty substitution; or guard the eval argument so an empty string never reaches it.
Fall back to a toolchain snapshot shipping m4 < 1.4.21 (e.g. an older Debian point release) while the macro is fixed.

non_solutions: Editing compiled C/C++ sources does not help; the failure happens in the macro layer before any C is compiled.
Passing -E / --fatal-warnings does not help; the eval error is fatal regardless.

summary: m4 1.4.21 broadened the `defn'-of-a-builtin concatenation warning to always fire (was inconsistent before), breaking autoregen under --fatal-warnings
mechanism: `defn(`builtin')' yields an opaque builtin token that can only be used as the sole argument of define/pushdef. m4 1.4.11 introduced a warning when such a token was concatenated with other text inside defn(...); m4 1.4.21 extended the check so define/pushdef ALWAYS warn (`Warning: cannot concatenate builtin ...') whenever the defn of a builtin is concatenated with anything, in any position. configure.ac/acinclude.m4 macros that wrote `define(`foo', `prefix'defn(`bar'))' previously worked silently on some m4 builds but now warn; combined with autoreconf's/autom4te's fatal-warnings handling the configure regeneration exits non-zero.

actions.hint: Re-write the macro so the defn() of a builtin is passed as a lone argument, e.g. change `define(`foo',`x'defn(`bar'))' to `define(`foo',defn(`bar'))' / push the builtin first then prepend the literal text via a second define, rather than concatenating.

If only the warning (not a real mis-expansion) is at stake, drop `--fatal-warnings'/`-E' from the m4/autom4te invocation (e.g. via the M4 / WARNINGS environment or AUTOM4TE_CFG) so the build proceeds while the macro is cleaned up.
Pin to m4 < 1.4.21 (older Debian stable) where the broader warning did not fire.

non_solutions: Quoting the concatenation differently does not silence it; the restriction is fundamental to how builtin tokens are represented.

summary: m4 1.4.8b made `eval' follow C precedence and deprecate `=' (formerly an alias for `=='); old m4 macros using `=' now warn and can mis-evaluate
mechanism: Before 1.4.8b, m4 `eval' accepted `=' as an undocumented alias for `==' and used non-C operator precedence. Since 1.4.8b eval follows C precedence and emits `Warning: recommend ==, not =, for equality operator' wherever `=' is used, reserving `=' for a future assignment extension. A configure.ac/acinclude.m4 macro that wrote `eval(A=B)' both changes meaning (precedence shift) and warns; under autoreconf's fatal-warnings the regeneration aborts.
trigger_patterns: Warning: recommend ==, not =, for equality operator

actions.hint: Replace every `=' used for equality with `==' inside eval() expressions in the project's m4 files (configure.ac, acinclude.m4, *.m4). While there, audit expressions that relied on the old precedence and add explicit parentheses.
Temporarily drop --fatal-warnings/-E from the m4 invocation (AUTOM4TE_CFG / M4 env) to let the warning through without aborting.

non_solutions: Wrapping the expression in quotes does not change eval tokenisation.

summary: m4 1.4.8b made `include' of a missing file set a non-zero exit status (POSIX); `sinclude' is the silent variant
mechanism: POSIX requires m4 to fail when an `include'd file cannot be opened. m4 1.4.8b changed `include' to honour this: a missing include target prints `cannot open `FILE'' and makes the overall m4 run (and thus autom4te/autoreconf) exit non-zero. Older m4 only warned and continued. Projects whose acinclude.m4 / configure.ac use `include(...)' for an optional local fragment therefore break the first time autoreconf runs against a modern m4 if that fragment is absent.
trigger_patterns: cannot open `.*': No such file or directory
autom4te: m4 failed with exit status

actions.hint: In the project m4 files, change `include(OPTIONAL)' to `sinclude(OPTIONAL)' for any include whose absence is acceptable; keep `include' only for mandatory fragments so a real omission is still caught.
Ensure the referenced file is actually generated before autoreconf (e.g. via aclocal's ACLOCAL_PATH / --acdir, or by touching the fragment in autogen.sh).

non_solutions: Adding the file to EXTRA_DIST does not help; the file must exist when m4 runs at autoreconf time.

summary: m4 1.4.6 made end-of-file inside a comment, quoted string or macro argument list a hard error
mechanism: Since 1.4.6 m4 diagnoses an input file that ends while still inside a comment block, a quoted string or an argument list, emitting `ERROR: end of file in comment', `ERROR: end of file in string' or `ERROR: end of file in argument list' and exiting non-zero. Older m4 silently tolerated an unterminated trailing comment (e.g. a configure.ac or .m4 file whose last line was a `#' comment with no terminating newline, or an unbalanced `changequote' pair). autoreconf against a modern m4 therefore aborts on inputs that built fine on m4 1.4.4/1.4.5.
trigger_patterns: end of file in argument list
negative_patterns: end of file treated as newline

actions.hint: Add a trailing newline to (and/or close the open construct in) the offending m4 input file (configure.ac, acinclude.m4, aclocal.m4 fragment, *.m4). The m4: header in the error names the file and the line where the dangling construct started.
If a changequote()/changecom() pair was left unbalanced, add the matching changequote()/changecom() to restore default delimiters at the end of the macro.

non_solutions: Re-running autoreconf does not help; the input itself is malformed.

summary: m4 1.4.5 requires frozen state files (m4 -F / -R) to begin with a `V' version directive; pre-1.4.5 frozen files are rejected
mechanism: A frozen state file (produced by `m4 -F' and reloaded by `m4 -R'/`--reload-state') produced by m4 before 1.4.5 lacks the leading `V' (version) directive that 1.4.5+ made mandatory. Reloading such a file now fails with `expecting character `V' in frozen file' (a truncated file instead yields `expecting line feed in frozen file', and a newer-than-supported format yields `frozen file version N greater than max supported of N' and exits with status 63). A project that ships a committed .m4f frozen state and runs `m4 -R file.m4f' during its build breaks when the distro upgrades m4.
trigger_patterns: expecting line feed in frozen file

actions.hint: Regenerate the frozen state file with the current m4 (`m4 -F new.m4f source.m4') and commit it, or stop shipping a frozen file and feed the plain .m4 text source into the build instead.
Keep an older m4 (Debian oldstable, < 1.4.5 era is unrealistic; in practice use the oldest m4 that accepted the legacy frozen format) solely for the reload step while migrating off frozen state.

non_solutions: Copying the old frozen file to a new name does not help; the directive is checked at reload time.

summary: m4 1.4.7 warns on the SysV-era spellings -e (use -i) and the no-op -B/-N/-S/-T/--diversions; -o/--error-output are still silently accepted (no warning).
mechanism: m4 1.4.7 retired SysV command-line compatibility as a goal. The compatibility option `-e' now warns (use `-i' for --interactive), and the no-op options `-B', `-N', `-S', `-T', `--diversions' now warn if used. (Note: `-o'/`--error-output' are still silently accepted but no longer documented; use `--debugfile'.) Wrapper scripts, autogen.sh or Makefile rules invoking m4 with the warning-emitting spellings now produce warnings and, under fatal-warnings / `set -e`, abort the build.

actions.hint: Update the m4 invocation in autogen.sh / Makefile / configure wrappers: replace `-e' with `-i', replace `-o FILE'/`--error-output=FILE' with `--debugfile=FILE', and drop the no-op `-B'/`-N'/`-S'/`-T'/`--diversions' arguments entirely.
If the invocation comes from autotools, set the M4 environment variable (or AUTOCONF's --M4 / autom4te.cfg) to point at a small wrapper script that rewrites the old spellings before exec'ing m4.

non_solutions: Suppressing the warning with --silent does not stop the exit-status change under fatal-warnings.

summary: Bundled config.sub is too old to recognize a modern CPU/architecture triplet component (aarch64, powerpc64le, riscv64, loongarch64, x86_64-gnux32), aborting configure before compilation.
mechanism: Old source releases vendor a historic config.sub from the GNU config project. When configure is invoked on a modern host (e.g. AArch64, RISC-V, LoongArch, ppc64le, x86_64 with x32 ABI), the canonical triplet sent to config.sub contains a CPU field that the historic script has no case-arm for, so it emits 'Invalid configuration `...': machine `...' not recognized' and exits 1. AC_CANONICAL_BUILD/HOST therefore fail and configure aborts, even though the toolchain itself supports the architecture. This is independent of the compiler and cannot be fixed by any C/C++ flag: only the build-system helper scripts need refreshing.

actions.hint: Refresh the vendored triplet scripts with current GNU config: copy up-to-date config.sub and config.guess from a modern autoconf/automake install over the project's copies, or run `automake --add-missing --force` / `autoreconf -fi` which pulls fresh copies from the system autotools.
Quick workaround without touching source: pass an explicit canonical triplet to configure, e.g. ./configure --build=$(gcc -dumpmachine) --host=$(gcc -dumpmachine), bypassing config.guess entirely.

non_solutions: upgrading gcc/binutils
adding -march=native
editing any .c/.cpp file

summary: Bundled config.sub predates the libc-suffix OS layer and rejects musl/relibc/uclibc/musleabihf triplets used by Alpine, embedded and cross-musl toolchains.
mechanism: Modern GNU config.sub splits the OS field into kernel+libc and recognizes composite OSes such as linux-musl, linux-uclibc, linux-relibc, linux-musleabihf. Historic config.sub releases have no case-arm for these libc suffixes and either reject the OS whole ('OS `linux-musl' not recognized') or, in transitional versions that introduced the libc concept but lack a matching entry, emit 'libc `...' needs explicit kernel' / 'Kernel `...' not known to work with OS `...'. The failure happens during triplet validation in configure (AC_CANONICAL_HOST), before any compilation, so no compiler flag can resolve it. Common on Alpine Linux, OpenWrt, Yocto musl, and Clang/musl cross toolchains.
trigger_patterns: Kernel `linux' not known to work with OS `linux-musl

actions.hint: Replace every vendored config.sub and config.guess in the source tree with current GNU config versions (>= 2014-05-01 for musl support, ideally latest), e.g. `wget -O config.sub 'https://git.savannah.gnu.org/cgit/config.git/plain/config.sub'` and likewise for config.guess, or run `autoreconf -fi` against a modern automake.

Cross-compile workaround: skip config.guess by giving configure the explicit canonical triplet, e.g. ./configure --host=aarch64-linux-musl --build=$(dpkg-architecture -qDEB_BUILD_GNU_TYPE 2>/dev/null || gcc -dumpmachine).

non_solutions: installing musl-dev
repointing CC to *-musl-gcc
editing compiled source

summary: Bundled config.guess cannot identify the build machine (new kernel/arch not in its uname tables), causing autoconf's configure to abort with 'cannot guess build type; you must specify one'.
mechanism: AC_CANONICAL_BUILD invokes config.guess to derive the build triplet from uname output. A historic config.guess has no mapping for a newer kernel version, CPU model string, or /proc layout, so its heuristics fall through and it prints 'config.guess: unable to guess system type' followed by a diagnostic dump and exit 1. Autoconf then terminates configure with 'configure: error: cannot guess build type; you must specify one' (and on cross-configures, 'configure: WARNING: If you wanted to set the build system type, you should use --build=...'). This is distinct from config.sub rejecting a triplet: here the GUESS step never produces a value. The fix is to refresh config.guess (and config.sub in tandem) or supply --build/--host explicitly.
trigger_patterns: configure: error: cannot guess build type
cannot guess build type; you must specify one
wanted to set the build system type

actions.hint: Replace the bundled config.guess (and its sibling config.sub) with current GNU config versions, or regenerate via `autoreconf -fi` / `automake --add-missing --force` so modern autotools install fresh copies.
Workaround without regenerating: pass the canonical triplet explicitly to skip config.guess, e.g. ./configure --build=$(uname -m)-linux-gnu or --build=$(gcc -dumpmachine).

non_solutions: upgrading the kernel
installing a newer GCC
modifying .c/.cpp sources

summary: libffi 3.3 removed FFI_SYSV enum value on x86_64
mechanism: libffi 3.3 removed FFI_SYSV from the ABI enum on amd64; code using FFI_SYSV on x86_64 fails with undeclared identifier error
trigger_patterns: 'FFI_SYSV' was not declared in this scope

actions.hint: -DFFI_SYSV=FFI_UNIX64 (on x86_64 only)
Use libffi < 3.3

non_solutions: Do not modify source

summary: Linux headers 5.2 moved SIOCGSTAMP definition requiring <linux/sockios.h>
mechanism: Linux headers 5.2 reorganized SIOCGSTAMP ioctl definition; code that previously got it from other headers now needs explicit #include <linux/sockios.h>
trigger_patterns: SIOCGSTAMP was not declared in this scope

actions.hint: -include linux/sockios.h
Use linux-headers < 5.2

summary: Source code calls POSIX group-database functions without #include <grp.h>; force-include via CFLAGS without editing source.
mechanism: Legacy C code that calls getgrnam/getgrgid/getgrnam/setgroups/initgroups without first including <grp.h> relies on a pre-C99 implicit declaration. On compilers that still allow it, the resulting code links because libc provides the symbols; on stricter compilers it fails at compile or link. The fix is to make the declaration visible via the compiler -include flag, which is a build-flag change (not a source edit).
negative_patterns: fatal error: grp.h: no such file or directory

actions.hint: Force-include grp.h via CFLAGS/CPPFLAGS so the declaration becomes visible without editing source. For autotools: ./configure CFLAGS="-include grp.h" or make CFLAGS="-D_GNU_SOURCE -include grp.h". For cmake: cmake -DCMAKE_C_FLAGS="-include grp.h" ..

non_solutions: Do NOT use -Wno-error=implicit-function-declaration: it silences the compiler but the linker still fails with 'undefined reference to getgrnam' because the declaration was never visible and the call site may have wrong arity.
Do NOT use -std=gnu89 here: the symbols are in libc, the problem is the missing declaration not the language standard.

summary: Source code calls mem* / str* functions without #include <cstring> (C++) or <string.h> (C); fix via -include flag.
mechanism: Pre-C99 / pre-C++98 code commonly called memcpy/memset/memmove/strlen/strcpy without including the corresponding header, relying on implicit declarations. Modern compilers reject this. Because the implementations live in libc/libstdc++, force-including the header via the compiler's -include flag makes the declaration visible and the link succeeds — no source edit required.
trigger_patterns: 'memcpy' was not declared in this scope
'memset' was not declared in this scope
'memmove' was not declared in this scope
'strlen' was not declared in this scope
'strcpy' was not declared in this scope
'strcmp' was not declared in this scope
'strerror' was not declared in this scope
negative_patterns: fatal error: string.h: no such file or directory
fatal error: cstring: no such file or directory

actions.hint: Force-include the string header. For C++: CXXFLAGS="-include cstring". For C: CFLAGS="-include string.h". For cmake: -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS="-include cstring" or -DCMAKE_C_FLAGS="-include string.h". For autotools: ./configure CXXFLAGS="-g -O2 -include cstring".

non_solutions: -Wno-error=implicit-function-declaration does NOT fix this: the call site still has no declaration, and on stricter toolchains the linker fails with 'undefined reference to memcpy'.
Do NOT switch sysuse or downgrade the compiler standard; libc has always provided these symbols — only the header inclusion is missing.

summary: Source code calls POSIX unistd functions (read/write/close/fork/chdir/getopt/environ) without #include <unistd.h>; fix via -include flag.
mechanism: Legacy C code commonly used POSIX functions from <unistd.h> without including the header. On older compilers this compiled via implicit declaration and linked against libc; on modern compilers it fails. Because the implementations are in libc, force-including <unistd.h> via CFLAGS makes the declarations visible without a source edit.
negative_patterns: fatal error: unistd.h: no such file or directory

actions.hint: Force-include unistd.h (and define _GNU_SOURCE for extensions like environ): CFLAGS="-D_GNU_SOURCE -include unistd.h". For autotools: ./configure CFLAGS="-D_GNU_SOURCE -include unistd.h". For make: make CFLAGS="-D_GNU_SOURCE -include unistd.h". For cmake: cmake -DCMAKE_C_FLAGS="-D_GNU_SOURCE -include unistd.h" ..

non_solutions: -Wno-error=implicit-function-declaration silences the compiler but does not make the declaration visible; on modern toolchains the call signature may mismatch and the linker can still fail.

summary: Source code uses wait/waitpid/WIFEXITED/WEXITSTATUS without #include <sys/wait.h>; fix via -include flag.
mechanism: Process-control macros and functions in <sys/wait.h> are sometimes called from legacy C without the include. The macros are header-only, the functions are in libc; both become available once the header is force-included via CFLAGS — no source edit needed.
negative_patterns: fatal error: sys/wait.h: no such file or directory

actions.hint: Force-include sys/wait.h: CFLAGS="-include sys/wait.h". For autotools: ./configure CFLAGS="-include sys/wait.h". For make: make CFLAGS="-include sys/wait.h". For cmake: cmake -DCMAKE_C_FLAGS="-include sys/wait.h" ..

non_solutions: -Wno-error=implicit-function-declaration does not help: WIFEXITED/WEXITSTATUS are macros defined in sys/wait.h; without the header they are simply absent and compilation fails regardless of warning level.

summary: Source code uses socket/bind/listen/accept/setsockopt/socklen_t without #include <sys/socket.h>; fix via -include flag.
mechanism: BSD-socket APIs live in <sys/socket.h>. Legacy code that omits the header compiles only via implicit declaration. Force-including the header via CFLAGS exposes the proper prototypes and types without a source edit.
negative_patterns: fatal error: sys/socket.h: no such file or directory

actions.hint: Force-include sys/socket.h (and netinet/in.h / arpa/inet.h if the source also uses sockaddr_in / inet_*): CFLAGS="-include sys/socket.h -include netinet/in.h -include arpa/inet.h".

non_solutions: -Wno-error=implicit-function-declaration will not define socklen_t/sa_family_t — those are typedefs in the header, not warnings.

summary: Source code uses errno/EAGAIN/EINVAL/EINTR without #include <errno.h>; fix via -include flag.
mechanism: errno is a macro/extern int declared in <errno.h>. Code that references it without the include fails to compile on modern toolchains. Force-including the header via CFLAGS resolves both the macro and the linker symbol without editing source.
negative_patterns: fatal error: errno.h: no such file or directory

actions.hint: Force-include errno.h: CFLAGS="-include errno.h". For make: make CFLAGS="-include errno.h". For autotools: ./configure CFLAGS="-include errno.h".

non_solutions: Switching sysuse does not help: errno.h has been part of every glibc release.

summary: Source code uses isspace/isalpha/isdigit/toupper/tolower without #include <ctype.h>; fix via -include flag.
mechanism: Character-classification functions in <ctype.h> are sometimes called without the include. Force-including the header via CFLAGS exposes the prototypes; libc provides the implementations — no source edit needed.
negative_patterns: fatal error: ctype.h: no such file or directory

actions.hint: Force-include ctype.h: CFLAGS="-include ctype.h" (C) or CXXFLAGS="-include cctype" (C++).

non_solutions: -Wno-error=implicit-function-declaration: the argument type (int) is benign here, but the cleaner fix is -include ctype.h which makes the prototype correct.

summary: A library changed its API/ABI between the project's era and the current toolchain. Symptoms: undeclared identifiers, struct member renamed/removed, function signature changed, incompatible pointer types, or implicit declaration of a function that used to be declared by a header.
mechanism: The project's source was written against the version of a library (e.g. tpm2-tss, libtiff, openssl, boost, rpm, mariadb) that shipped in its commit-era Debian release. The current sysuse provides a different version whose headers/libraries expose a different API surface. The fix is NOT to edit the source — instead pick a dependency version that matches the project's era: (1) a different package name that carries the legacy API, (2) an older or newer Debian suite whose repository has the matching version, or (3) build the dep from source at a tag close to the project's commit date.
trigger_patterns: was not declared in this scope
was not declared in this scope

actions.hint: Identify the offending library from the error (file path / #include / symbol prefix). Then enumerate available versions with `apt-cache madison <libname>* | sort` and `apt-cache search <libname>`. Pick a version close to the project's commit era. The Phase 3 agent decides next step after seeing probe output: try alt_pkg (versioned variant like libtiff4-dev vs libtiff5-dev, bundle like libboost-all-dev, or *-compat), or switch sysuse, or build the dep from source.

non_solutions: Editing the project's .c/.h/.cpp source to rename symbols — the constraint forbids modifying source

summary: The build is blocked by toolchain behavior that the project did not anticipate and that cannot be disabled with a clean build_flag: project hard-codes -Werror in a Makefile/configure.ac, the build expects a tool that no longer exists under its old name (gcc-4.1, aclocal-1.11, libtoolize from libtool 1.x), or a wrapper script is needed to inject the right flags.
mechanism: Some projects bake strict error handling or hard-coded tool paths into their build files in ways that a CMAKE_C_FLAGS / CFLAGS / --disable-* knob cannot reach. In those cases the cheapest non-invasive fix is to interpose a tiny wrapper script between the build system and the real tool: the wrapper rewrites argv to add -Wno-error / -fpermissive / -fcommon, or maps gcc-4.1 -> gcc, then exec's the real tool. The wrapper lives under /tmp/ so the project source tree is untouched.

actions.hint: First try the canonical flag through the build system's standard knob: CFLAGS/CXXFLAGS += -Wno-error (or -Wno-error=<specific> for surgical suppression), or -fpermissive to downgrade C++ errors to warnings, or -fcommon for GCC 10+ multiple-definition errors, or -fno-sanitize-recover=all for sanitizer-trap errors. Only fall back to tool_shim if the build system has NO flag knob that reaches the failing target.

Write a wrapper script under /tmp/ that intercepts the failing tool and rewrites its arguments. Example for a project that hard-codes gcc-4.1 and -Werror:
  cat > /tmp/shim-cc.sh <<'SHIM'
  #!/bin/sh
  exec gcc -Wno-error -fpermissive "$@"
  SHIM
  chmod +x /tmp/shim-cc.sh
  export CC=/tmp/shim-cc.sh
  export CXX=/tmp/shim-cxx.sh  # (analogous wrapper for g++)
Then re-run ./configure && make. Works because the build system invokes $CC / $CXX; the project source is untouched. For autotools projects that hard-code the tool name in Makefile.in (not via $CC), symlink the wrapper into a directory on PATH under the expected name (e.g. ln -s /tmp/shim-cc.sh /usr/local/bin/gcc-4.1).

non_solutions: Prefer tool_shim over editing build files — tool_shim is cheaper and doesn't require re-running autoreconf
Switching sysuse just to dodge -Werror — older sysuse will likely also lack the legacy tool name

summary: apt install failed because the requested package set mixes mutually exclusive providers or packages unavailable in the current Debian suite.
mechanism: Phase 1 dependency extraction can over-include alternatives such as two Kerberos implementations, two curl TLS variants, or old/new pkg-config providers. apt then reports held broken packages, Conflicts, or not-going-to-be-installed errors. The repair is to install one verified provider per family for the current suite, not to repeat the same package list.
trigger_patterns: but it is not going to be installed

actions.hint: Inspect the failed apt-get install command and shrink it to one provider from each conflicting family. Verify the chosen provider in the current Debian suite with Verify_Package or apt-cache policy. Re-run apt-get install with the reduced list, then clean/reconfigure/rebuild.

non_solutions: Do not retry the exact same apt-get install package list.
Do not switch sysuse before testing a reduced single-provider package set in the current suite.

summary: The build needs a source-built dependency, vendored directory, submodule, or sibling SDK rather than another apt package retry.
mechanism: Errors that reference third_party/deps/vendor/external paths, missing submodule files, package metadata unavailable in apt, or a required dependency version absent from the suite need an executable source_dependency plan. The plan must tell Phase 2 where the dependency source lives, how to build it, where it installs, and which environment exports expose it to the main build.
trigger_patterns: Could not find a package configuration file provided by

actions.hint: Return status=source_dependency with source_dependency containing name, container_source_path or source_path/submodule_path, setup_commands/fetch_commands when needed, non-empty build_order, install_prefix, and env_exports for PKG_CONFIG_PATH/LD_LIBRARY_PATH/CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH/include paths. Preserve the target project commit; do not checkout target repo main/master.

non_solutions: Do not solve missing vendored/submodule paths by installing unrelated apt packages.
Do not replace the target checkout with a floating branch.

summary: The command is running in the wrong directory or building the wrong target; switch to a high-confidence entrypoint candidate or component target.
mechanism: Many repositories expose multiple build systems, generated wrappers, component subdirectories, or examples/tests. Repeating root cmake/make after no Makefile, no CMakeLists, no target, or wrong-directory errors wastes turns. Use build_plan entrypoint candidates and wrapper scripts as the next action.
trigger_patterns: No targets specified and no makefile found
does not appear to contain CMakeLists.txt

actions.hint: Inspect build_plan_summary.entrypoints, command_candidates, and available_wrappers. Try the highest-confidence doc/script candidate or cd into the subdir that owns the build file. If the project is a huge monorepo, build the component target implied by the failing file instead of the whole tree.

non_solutions: Do not repeat the same failed root build command.
Do not install packages before confirming the command is pointed at a real build entrypoint.

summary: The next repair should be a build-layer compatibility flag, dependency-version alignment, or tool shim rather than editing project source.
mechanism: Legacy C/C++ projects often fail under newer compilers due to -Werror, implicit declarations, -fno-common, removed warning options, stricter C++ conversions, or linker behavior. The preferred repair is to pass flags through the build system or interpose a wrapper tool; source edits are not allowed.
negative_patterns: fatal error: .* No such file or directory

actions.hint: Try the build-system-specific flag path first: CFLAGS/CXXFLAGS/CPPFLAGS/LDFLAGS/LIBS, cmake CMAKE_C_FLAGS/CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS, meson -Dc_args/-Dcpp_args, or make VAR=value. Common flags include -Wno-error, -Wno-error=<specific>, -fcommon, -fpermissive, and explicit LIBS/LDFLAGS ordering. If the build system hard-codes the tool/flags, use tool_shim.
Create a /tmp wrapper for CC/CXX/LD/AR/MAKE that rewrites unsupported or strict flags, export the tool variable, clean the build cache, and rebuild.

non_solutions: Do not edit .c/.h/.cpp files.
Do not keep installing packages when the failure is a compiler/linker policy change.

summary: A C++ dependency API returns a view/proxy type such as string_view while this project expects an owning string or reference type.
mechanism: Newer dependency headers may change return types from std::string-like values to std::string_view, boost::basic_string_view, span, or other view/proxy objects. Legacy project code then fails with reference initialization, binding, or conversion errors even though all headers are present. This is usually dependency API drift, not a missing package or a compiler flag issue. Align the dependency version with the project era via an alternate package, a more suitable sysuse, or a source-built dependency.
trigger_patterns: invalid initialization of reference of type
cannot bind rvalue reference of type

actions.hint: Identify the dependency from the namespace, include path, or failing type (for example libtorrent::string_view implies libtorrent-rasterbar). Query the installed and available dependency versions with pkg-config --modversion when available, apt-cache policy, apt-cache madison, and apt-cache search for versioned or compatibility packages. Prefer the project-era dependency version: try a verified alternate package or switch sysuse when apt provides a matching version; if apt cannot provide it, return a source_dependency plan that builds the dependency at a tag close to the target project's commit date and exports PKG_CONFIG_PATH/CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH/LD_LIBRARY_PATH.

non_solutions: Do not edit project .c/.h/.cpp files to wrap the view type in std::string.
Do not install unrelated generic Boost packages when the failing type comes from a dependency API return type.
Do not use -fpermissive as the primary fix for incompatible reference initialization.
